why.correct: Every organ is built from just four tissue types: epithelial tissue covers and lines, the connective type supports and binds, muscle contracts, and nervous tissue carries electrical signals.
options: Correct. These are the four primary tissue types.
Glands are made mostly of epithelial cells, so they are a kind of epithelium, not a separate primary type. The connective type is missing from this list.
Skeleton and blood are both kinds of the connective type; they are not separate primary types. Muscle and nervous tissue are missing.
These are cell shapes and one subtype used to name epithelia. They are all kinds of one tissue type, not four different types.

why.correct: The apical surface (apex = tip) is the free face of an epithelial cell. It looks into a lumen, such as the inside of the trachea, or out to the environment. Microvilli and cilia sit on this face.
options: The face on the basement membrane is the basal surface, the opposite of the apical surface.
The capillaries lie below the basement membrane, on the basal side. Nutrients reach the cell through its basal surface.
Correct. The apical surface faces the open space or the outside world.
The sides of the cell face neighbors and carry the tight junctions and desmosomes. They are the lateral surfaces, not the apical surface.

why.correct: Avascular means without blood vessels (a- = without, vascul- = small vessel). Epithelial cells receive oxygen and nutrients by diffusion from capillaries in the tissue below the basement membrane.
options: Most epithelial cells have nuclei. Only the dead surface cells of keratinized epithelium have lost them.
Correct. Epithelium has no blood vessels of its own.
Epithelium renews itself constantly; its deep cells divide to replace cells lost from the surface.
Epithelium is firmly attached to the tissue below by the basement membrane.

why.correct: One layer of flat cells is simple squamous epithelium. The simple squamous lining of the heart and blood vessels has its own name: endothelium (endo- = within).
options: Mesothelium is also simple squamous, but it is the surface layer of a serous membrane such as the pleura, not a vessel lining.
Transitional epithelium is many layers thick and lines the urinary passages, not blood vessels.
Cuboidal cells are about as tall as they are wide. The cells here are flat.
Correct. Endothelium is the simple squamous lining of the heart and blood vessels.

why.correct: Diffusion is fastest over the shortest distance. A single layer of flat cells gives the thinnest barrier, which is why the air sacs of your lungs are lined with simple squamous epithelium.
options: Many layers of cells make a thick barrier, which slows diffusion. Stratified squamous suits surfaces that are rubbed, not exchange surfaces.
Tall cells make a longer path than flat ones. Their many mitochondria power active transport, which a gas crossing by diffusion does not need.
Correct. A thin, single layer of flat cells gives the shortest diffusion distance.
Transitional epithelium is several layers thick even when stretched, and it lines urinary organs. Stretch does not make diffusion fast.

why.correct: The test for layers is contact with the basement membrane. If every cell touches it, the epithelium is one layer. Cells of different heights put their nuclei at different levels, so the sheet looks stratified but is not.
options: Rows of nuclei are not layers of cells. In a stratified epithelium, the upper cells do not touch the basement membrane, and here every cell does.
Correct. Every cell touching the basement membrane means one layer; the varied heights make it look layered.
Transitional epithelium is truly stratified and lines the urinary passages. Its surface cells do not touch the basement membrane.
The name follows the cells that reach the surface. Here those cells are tall, so the tissue is columnar.

why.correct: Every epithelium is a sheet of closely joined cells with an apical and a basal surface, resting on a basement membrane. None has its own blood vessels, and many are only one layer thick.
options: Correct. Tight junctions and desmosomes hold epithelial cells tightly together.
Correct. Every epithelial cell has a free apical face and a basal face toward deeper tissue.
Epithelium is avascular. Its vessels are in the tissue below the basement membrane.
Correct. Every epithelium rests on a basement membrane.
Simple epithelia are a single layer, so layering is not shared by all.

why.correct: The basement membrane is a mat of proteins outside the cells. The basal lamina is made by the epithelial cells; the reticular lamina, a net of thin fibers, is made by cells of the tissue underneath.
options: These are the two faces of an epithelial cell, not layers of the basement membrane.
These are the two main layers of the skin. The epidermis sits on a basement membrane that separates it from the dermis.
Correct. Basal lamina plus reticular lamina make the basement membrane.
These are two named kinds of simple squamous epithelium, not parts of the basement membrane.

why.correct: In respiratory epithelium, goblet cells release mucus that traps particles, and cilia beat in waves that carry the mucus toward the throat. Without cilia, the mucus pools, and coughing becomes the only way to clear it.
options: Gas exchange happens across the thin lining of the air sacs, not across the trachea.
Correct. Cilia move the mucus sheet; lose them and mucus builds up.
Goblet cells still make mucus, often more of it in smokers. The problem is moving it, not making it.
The trachea is a fairly rigid tube and does not rely on stretchy epithelium. Transitional epithelium, which stretches, lines the urinary passages.

why.correct: Swallowed food scrapes the esophagus, and its lining has many layers of cells, so worn surface cells are replaced from below. The surface stays wet, and its surface cells stay alive. It has no dead, keratin-filled layer like the one on your skin.
options: Correct. Many layers take the wear, and the wet surface cells stay alive.
The esophagus moves food along; it does not absorb nutrients.
Food scrapes the esophagus with every swallow, and its many layers of cells take that wear.
That describes keratinized epithelium, such as the surface of your skin. In the esophagus the surface cells stay alive and moist.

why.correct: Mucus has to be on the surface before anything can stick to it. The cilia then move the loaded mucus sheet upward, and it ends up in the throat, where it is swallowed.
Transitional epithelium stretches. As the bladder fills, its cells slide past one another and flatten, so the sheet thins without tearing. When the bladder empties, the cells round up again.
options: Losing cells every time the bladder filled would strip the lining. The cells stay in place and change shape.
The ureters, bladder and first part of the urethra are all lined by the same transitional epithelium. The change comes from stretch.
Correct. The cells flatten and rearrange as the wall stretches.
The surface cells seal tightly and block water movement between urine and the wall. The change is in shape, not water content.

why.correct: Without vessels of its own, epithelium depends on diffusion from capillaries in the tissue beneath. Diffusion is fastest over short distances, so the cells nearest the basement membrane get the best supply.
options: Correct. Diffusion from capillaries below links the missing vessels to the well-supplied deep cells.
Human cells cannot make glucose from carbon dioxide. They depend on nutrients delivered by the blood.
Surface cells may be dead or far from any supply. Nutrients come from below, not from the air.
The basement membrane is a protein mat with no blood flowing in it. Nutrients diffuse through it.

why.correct: Epithelium is avascular. There are no vessels between the cells of the epidermis, so cells moving up get farther from their supply, not closer to it.
options: This step is right: the best-supplied cells, at the base, are the ones that divide.
This step is right: new cells push older ones upward.
This step is right: in keratinized epithelium, rising cells fill with keratin.
This is the error. The epidermis has no blood vessels; its supply diffuses up from capillaries in the dermis.
This step is right: the dead keratin-filled cells shed and are replaced from below.

why.correct: Active transport needs ATP and many transport proteins. Cube-shaped cells have room for mitochondria and other organelles, and microvilli add membrane area. One layer keeps the path short.
options: A dry, dead, many-layered surface would block transport. It suits the skin, not a tubule.
This lining moves mucus with cilia in the airways. It does not do the absorbing a tubule needs.
Transitional epithelium stretches and seals in urine; it is not built for absorbing.
Correct. Simple cuboidal cells, many with microvilli, line the kidney tubules.

variables.name: Resistance of the lining to physical irritation
variables.why: Stratified squamous epithelium has many layers of cells, so damage to the surface cells leaves deeper cells intact.

variables.name: Number of cilia on the surface
variables.why: Stratified squamous cells have no cilia, so the new lining cannot beat mucus upward.

variables.name: Mucus released onto the surface by goblet cells
variables.why: The new lining has no goblet cells, so less mucus reaches the surface in those patches.

variables.name: Clearing of trapped particles from those patches
variables.why: With no goblet cells to trap particles and no cilia to move mucus, particles stay where they land.

why.correct: Goblet cells are cup-shaped cells scattered in columnar epithelia. They fill with mucus, a slippery gel, and release it onto the surface by exocytosis.
options: Keratin is a tough protein that builds up inside cells of keratinized epithelium. It is not released.
Serous fluid comes from mesothelium, the simple squamous surface of serous membranes.
Correct. Goblet cells release mucus.
Urine is made by the kidneys and carried away through tubes lined with transitional epithelium.

why.correct: Swallowed food scrapes the upper surface of the epiglottis, so it has a many-layered lining. The surface is moist, so it is nonkeratinized. Lower on its airway side, where food does not scrape, the lining becomes respiratory epithelium.
options: A single flat layer would be scraped away by food. Simple squamous suits exchange surfaces.
Respiratory epithelium does cover the lower part of the epiglottis's airway side, where food does not scrape. On the food-facing surface, cilia and a single layer would be worn away.
Transitional epithelium stretches and lines urinary organs, not the throat.
Correct. Many layers resist wear, and the moist surface does not keratinize.

why.correct: Connective tissue is mostly matrix: ground substance and fibers made by relatively few, scattered cells. The matrix gives each connective tissue its properties.
options: Cells packed edge to edge describe epithelium, the opposite arrangement.
Correct. Scattered cells in abundant extracellular matrix define connective tissue.
Shortening to pull is the job of muscle, the tissue type covered in the next topic.
A free apical surface facing a lumen belongs to epithelium. Connective tissue sits inside the body with no free surface.

why.correct: The matrix is made of ground substance, a water-holding gel, plus protein fibers (collagen, elastic and reticular) running through it. Cells sit in the matrix but are not part of it.
options: These are cells that live in connective tissue. They make or clean the matrix; they are not the matrix itself.
These are parts of blood. Plasma is blood's matrix, but platelets are cell fragments, not matrix.
These are the two parts of the basement membrane under an epithelium.
Correct. Ground substance plus fibers make up the extracellular matrix.

why.correct: Elastic fibers are built mainly of elastin, whose molecules uncoil when stretched and recoil when released. They can stretch to about one and a half times their length.
options: Collagen fibers are very strong when pulled, but they barely stretch.
Reticular fibers are thin collagen strands that form supporting nets. They do not recoil like elastin.
Correct. Elastic fibers stretch and recoil.
Keratin fills cells of keratinized epithelium. It is not a connective tissue fiber.

why.correct: Fibroblasts (fibro- = fiber, -blast = builder) make collagen, elastic and reticular fibers and the ground substance. A less active one that maintains the matrix is called a fibrocyte.
options: Correct. Fibroblasts build the matrix of connective tissue proper.
Macrophages engulf debris and bacteria. They clean the tissue; they don't build its matrix.
Adipocytes store triglyceride in fat droplets.
Chondrocytes make the matrix of cartilage, a supportive connective tissue, not connective tissue proper.

why.correct: Macrophages (macro- = large, phag- = eat) engulf bacteria, dead cells and debris and digest them in lysosomes. Many come from a type of white blood cell that settles in tissues. You'll meet them again in the immune system chapter.
options: Fibroblasts make fibers and ground substance. They don't engulf bacteria.
Adipocytes store fat. They don't engulf bacteria.
Correct. Macrophages are the phagocytes of connective tissue.
Chondrocytes live only in cartilage and build its matrix.

why.correct: Tendons are dense regular connective tissue: thick collagen bundles lined up in one direction. Collagen is very strong in tension, so the tendon is strong along its fibers and weak across them.
options: Tendons are mostly collagen, not elastic fibers, and their strength comes from how the collagen is lined up.
Correct. Parallel collagen bundles resist pulling along their length.
Dense connective tissue has little ground substance. Ground substance doesn't resist pulling.
Tendon cells are fibroblasts, which don't contract. The force comes from the muscle the tendon is attached to.

why.correct: Dense irregular tissue has thick collagen bundles running in many directions, so it resists pulls from any direction. That is the dermis's tissue.
options: Dense regular tissue resists pulling in one direction only. It suits tendons and ligaments.
Reticular tissue is a delicate net that supports soft organs such as the spleen. It is not strong.
Hyaline cartilage resists squeezing and is avascular. The dermis is a flexible, well-supplied layer.
Correct. Collagen bundles running every way resist stretch from any direction.

why.correct: Loose connective tissue has few, loosely woven fibers and plenty of ground substance. Its three forms are areolar, adipose and reticular tissue.
options: Correct. Areolar tissue is the loose packing under epithelia.
Correct. Adipose tissue is loose connective tissue filled with fat cells.
A tendon is dense regular connective tissue, packed with parallel collagen.
Correct. Reticular tissue is a loose net of reticular fibers in soft organs.
Fibrocartilage is a supportive connective tissue, a kind of cartilage.

why.correct: A ligament is dense regular connective tissue that joins one bone to another where they meet, holding them together.
options: Correct. Ligaments join bone to bone.
A tendon connects muscle to bone.
Muscles can meet through flat sheets of tendon (aponeuroses), but a ligament joins bones.
Skin is anchored by the dermis and the loose tissue below it, not by ligaments.

why.correct: Cartilage is avascular, so repair depends on slow diffusion and a few slow-dividing chondrocytes. Bone has a rich blood supply that brings cells and nutrients to a break, so it heals in weeks.
options: Menisci are fibrocartilage, not elastic cartilage. The healing problem is the missing blood supply.
Bone is living tissue with cells throughout its matrix; its blood supply is what lets it heal.
Correct. No vessels in the inner meniscus means little repair; bone's rich supply supports healing.
Fibrocartilage has no perichondrium at all. A perichondrium would actually help, since it carries vessels and cells.

why.correct: Elastic cartilage has a dense web of elastic fibers in its matrix, so it bends and springs back. It shapes the ear flap and the epiglottis.
options: Hyaline cartilage is only slightly flexible. It forms the tip of the nose and the rings of the trachea.
Fibrocartilage is packed with thick collagen and resists compression and pulling. It forms intervertebral discs and menisci.
Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage on bone ends where they meet and glide.
Correct. Elastic cartilage gives the ear flap its bend-and-return flexibility.

why.correct: All cartilage resists squeezing because its ground substance holds water. Fibrocartilage adds thick bundles of collagen, which resist pulling. A disc faces both, so it is fibrocartilage.
options: Correct. Collagen bundles add strength in tension to cartilage's resistance to compression.
Cartilage matrix has almost no blood vessels. Only the outer rim of pads such as the menisci gets a small supply.
Elastic cartilage is the most flexible type. Fibrocartilage is the toughest.
Hyaline cartilage is the most common cartilage in adults too, for example on bone ends and in the trachea.

why.correct: The electron transport chain still runs and still uses oxygen, but the hydrogen ions it pumps flow back without driving ATP production. The energy in that gradient is lost as heat, which warms the body.
options: Letting the ions leak back bypasses ATP production, so less ATP is made, not more.
Correct. The energy is released as heat instead of being captured in ATP.
Brown fat cells store fat in many small droplets. The single large droplet is typical of white fat.
The electron transport chain keeps running, so oxygen use continues and can even rise.

why.correct: Damage comes first. Platelets gather at the site, then the dissolved protein forms threads that bind the platelet mass and trap cells into a clot. The blood chapter covers the full sequence.
In any connective tissue, cells sit in an extracellular matrix. In blood, that matrix is plasma, a liquid of water, salts, nutrients and dissolved proteins.
options: Red cells are the most numerous cells of blood. They sit in the matrix; they are not the matrix.
Platelets are cell fragments carried in the matrix.
Correct. Plasma is blood's liquid matrix.
White cells are cells carried by blood, not its matrix.

why.correct: Mesenchyme (mes- = middle) is loose embryonic connective tissue of star-shaped stem cells in a watery ground substance. Its cells differentiate into fibroblasts, fat cells, chondrocytes and the cells of bone.
options: That is the perichondrium, a layer of dense irregular tissue.
Correct. Mesenchyme is embryonic connective tissue made of stem cells.
That is the basement membrane.
That describes brown adipose tissue.

why.correct: Cartilage is avascular. There are no capillaries in its matrix; oxygen and nutrients must diffuse through the matrix to reach the chondrocytes.
options: This step is right: the perichondrium carries the vessels that supply most cartilage.
This step is right: supplies leave the vessels outside the cartilage.
This is the error. Cartilage has no capillaries; supplies diffuse through the matrix.
This step is right: diffusion makes the central cells the least supplied.
This step is right: a poor supply and few slow cells make repair slow.

why.correct: Cartilage's ground substance is packed with large molecules that hold water. A load squeezes some water out, and the water flows back when the load is removed. That makes cartilage a shock absorber.
options: Correct. Load pushes water out of the ground substance.
Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage, with few elastic fibers, and recoil would restore shape, not flatten it.
Chondrocytes cannot contract; they maintain the matrix.
Cartilage has no capillaries.

variables.name: Strength of tendons and ligaments when pulled
variables.why: Tendons and ligaments get their strength in tension from parallel collagen bundles, so weaker collagen makes them easier to overstretch or tear.

variables.name: Resistance of the dermis to tearing
variables.why: The dermis is dense irregular tissue built from collagen bundles, so weaker collagen lets the skin tear or bruise more easily.

variables.name: Ability of bone to resist bending without breaking
variables.why: Collagen gives bone its flexibility; with weak collagen, the mineral matrix is more brittle and breaks more easily.

why.correct: Each skeletal muscle fiber forms in the embryo when many small cells fuse end to end. The fused fiber is long and keeps all their nuclei, which sit just under its plasma membrane.
options: Smooth muscle fibers are small and spindle-shaped, with a single nucleus in the center.
Cardiac fibers are short and branched, with one central nucleus (occasionally two).
Correct. Long, cylindrical, multinucleated fibers with nuclei at the edge are skeletal muscle.
Visceral muscle is another name for smooth muscle, which has one central nucleus per fiber.

why.correct: An intercalated disc is the zigzag joint where two cardiac fibers meet end to end. It holds desmosomes and gap junctions, and it shows as a dark line across the fibers in a stained slide.
options: Correct. Intercalated discs join cardiac fibers end to end.
A skeletal fiber attaches to its tendon through collagen, not through intercalated discs. Skeletal fibers have no discs.
Smooth muscle fibers have no intercalated discs; where they are linked, it is by gap junctions between fibers.
A skeletal fiber is one continuous cell, so there are no joints between its nuclei.

why.correct: Both are striated, because both stack actin and myosin in lined-up repeating units. They differ in control, nuclei and junctions.
options: Correct. Both show the light and dark bands of striated muscle.
Only skeletal muscle is voluntary. You cannot make your heart beat by deciding to.
Correct. Every muscle tissue, smooth included, contracts using actin and myosin.
Only skeletal fibers have many nuclei at the edge. A cardiac fiber usually has one nucleus in its center.
Only cardiac muscle has intercalated discs.

why.correct: Branched, striated fibers with central nuclei and intercalated discs (the dark zigzag lines) are cardiac muscle, which is found only in the heart wall.
options: The biceps is skeletal muscle: unbranched fibers with many nuclei at the edge and no discs.
Correct. Only cardiac muscle has branched striated fibers joined by intercalated discs.
The stomach wall is smooth muscle, which has no striations.
The bladder wall is smooth muscle: spindle-shaped fibers with no striations and no discs.

why.correct: Resistance is proportional to 1 / radius to the fourth power. Half the radius gives (1/2) to the fourth = 1/16 of the starting radius-to-the-fourth, so resistance becomes 16 times larger.
options: Doubling would be true only if resistance depended on the radius itself, not its fourth power.
Four times would come from squaring the radius. Resistance depends on the fourth power.
Correct. (1/2) to the fourth power is 1/16, so resistance rises 16-fold.
A narrower vessel has more resistance to flow, not less.

why.correct: Vasoconstriction narrows the vessels, resistance rises with the fourth power of the radius, flow falls, and less warm blood reaches the skin, so the fingers turn pale and cold.

variables.name: Radius of the small arteries
variables.why: Contracting smooth muscle rings squeeze the vessel narrower: vasoconstriction.

variables.name: Resistance to blood flow in those arteries
variables.why: Resistance rises steeply as radius falls, with the fourth power of the radius.

variables.name: Blood flow into the fingers
variables.why: With the pressure gradient about the same, higher resistance means lower flow.

variables.name: Skin temperature of the fingers
variables.why: Less warm blood reaches the fingers, so they cool toward the outside air.

why.correct: Cardiac muscle is striated but involuntary. Striation describes how the filaments are arranged; voluntary describes how contraction is controlled.
options: Thigh muscle is striated and voluntary, so it fits the claim instead of disproving it.
Intestinal smooth muscle is involuntary, but it is also nonstriated, so it says nothing about striated muscle.
Vessel smooth muscle is nonstriated, so it cannot test a claim about striated muscle.
Correct. Cardiac muscle is striated yet you cannot make it contract by choice.

why.correct: Ions pass between cardiac fibers through gap junctions, the channels in the intercalated discs. Desmosomes are anchoring junctions that hold the fibers together; they have no channel for ions.
options: This step is right: the process starts with an electrical change in one fiber.
This is the error. Ions cross through gap junctions. Desmosomes rivet cells together and pass nothing between them.
This step is right: the incoming ions trigger the same change and contraction in the neighbor.
This step is right: each fiber passes the change on, so it sweeps across the region.
This step is right: desmosomes keep the contracting fibers from tearing apart.

why.correct: Contraction of the smooth muscle fibers tightens the ring around the vessel, which shrinks its radius. A smaller radius raises resistance sharply, and with the same pressure gradient, flow falls.
Gap junctions in the intercalated disc connect the cytoplasm of the two fibers. Ions carrying the electrical change pass straight through them into the neighbor.
options: Correct. Gap junctions carry the ions from fiber to fiber.
Desmosomes hold fibers together mechanically. They do not carry electrical changes.
Cardiac fibers stay separate cells joined at discs. Fusion into one cell happens in developing skeletal muscle.
The heart has no tendons between its fibers; the fibers are joined directly at intercalated discs.

why.correct: Extensibility (ex- = out, tend- = stretch) is the ability to be stretched beyond resting length without damage.
options: Elasticity is recoil back to resting length after a stretch, the opposite half of the story.
Correct. Being stretched without damage is extensibility.
Responsiveness is reacting to signals with an electrical change across the membrane.
Contraction is active shortening, not being stretched.

why.correct: Elasticity is the ability to recoil to resting length once a stretching force is removed. The released strip springs back on its own.
options: Extensibility is the ability to be stretched, which happened when the strip was pulled. The return afterward is recoil.
Responsiveness needs a signal, and no stimulus was given.
Correct. Recoil to resting length after stretch is elasticity.
Bladder smooth muscle is involuntary, and this recoil is passive.

why.correct: About 1% or fewer of cardiac fibers are replaced each year, and fewer with age. Dead fibers leave gaps that fibroblasts fill with collagen, which cannot contract. Skeletal muscle has stem cells beside its fibers that multiply and repair damage.
options: The heart wall has a rich blood supply. The damage happened because one artery was blocked, not because the tissue lacks vessels.
Correct. Cardiac fibers are almost never replaced, so a noncontracting collagen patch replaces them.
Cardiac muscle is striated. Striation has nothing to do with replacing lost fibers.
Repair depends on stem cells beside the fibers, not on voluntary control.

why.correct: Smooth muscle, also called visceral muscle, forms the walls of hollow organs such as the intestines, stomach, bladder, uterus, airways and blood vessels.
options: Correct. The intestinal wall contains layers of smooth muscle.
The muscle that bends your elbow is skeletal muscle attached to bone by tendons.
The heart wall is cardiac muscle.
The eye-moving muscles are skeletal muscles; you can move your eyes by choice.

why.correct: Stripes appear only when actin and myosin are stacked in short repeating units lined up across the fiber. In smooth muscle, the filaments crisscross at angles, so no bands line up.
options: Smooth fibers have one nucleus each. Nuclei do not create or hide striations anyway.
Control does not create stripes. Cardiac muscle is involuntary and still striated.
Correct. Filament arrangement, not filament type, decides whether stripes show.
Smooth muscle has both actin and myosin; that is how it contracts.

why.correct: You cannot make your heart or your stomach contract by choice. Both cardiac and smooth muscle respond to the nervous system, blood chemicals and local conditions.
options: Skeletal muscle is voluntary: you can start its contractions by choice.
Correct. Cardiac muscle beats with no decision on your part.
Correct. Smooth muscle in organ and vessel walls is not under conscious control.

why.correct: Contraction means myosin pulling actin filaments so the fiber shortens. A shortening cell can pull but cannot push, so a different muscle on the back of the arm pulls the elbow straight.
options: Strength is not the issue. No muscle of any strength can push.
ATP powers the pulling of actin by myosin. There is no pushing action to power.
Holding the elbow bent takes the front muscle contracting, not relaxing, and relaxing cannot push anything. The muscle on the back of the arm straightens the elbow by pulling.
Correct. Muscle only pulls; opposing muscles move a joint back.

why.correct: In the embryo, many small muscle-forming cells line up and fuse end to end. The fused fiber keeps every nucleus.
options: Correct. Fusion of many embryonic cells gives each skeletal fiber its many nuclei.
This describes a different route to many nuclei. Skeletal fibers get theirs by fusion.
Stem cells beside the fibers can later fuse with damaged fibers for repair, but that is not how a fiber first forms.
Nuclei do not travel through the blood into muscle fibers.

why.correct: Gap junctions pass the electrical change from fiber to fiber. Without them, each fiber would contract on its own timing, so the region could not squeeze as a unit.
options: Desmosomes hold the fibers together, and they are left intact.
Correct. Without gap junctions, the electrical change cannot spread, so fibers lose coordination.
Striations come from filament arrangement inside each fiber, which the drug does not touch.
Uncoordinated fibers pull against one another, so the wall squeezes less effectively, not more.

why.correct: Nervous tissue has neurons, which carry signals, and glial cells, which support and protect them.
options: Fibroblasts are the main cells of connective tissue proper, not nervous tissue.
Correct. Neurons and glial cells are the two cell types of nervous tissue.
Muscle fibers belong to muscle tissue, the third primary tissue type.
A nerve is a bundle of axons, and an axon is part of a neuron. Neither is a separate kind of cell.

why.correct: Dendrites (dendr- = tree) are short, branched extensions of the cell body. Their branches receive signals from the axon terminals of other neurons.
options: The axon carries the neuron's own signal away from the cell body.
Axon terminals send signals to the next cell by releasing chemicals.
Correct. Dendrites receive incoming signals.
The nucleus holds DNA and directs protein making; it does not receive signals from other cells.

why.correct: Each neuron has one axon, and it carries the signal away from the cell body to the axon terminals at its far end.
options: That path belongs to the dendrites, which bring signals in toward the cell body.
Correct. The axon carries signals away from the cell body.
This runs the path backward. Signals leave through the axon terminals; they do not return along the axon.
A neuron carries signals one way: in through dendrites, out through the axon.

why.correct: Signals come in through the dendrites, are combined in the cell body, leave along the axon, and are passed on by the axon terminals.
The cell body holds the nucleus and most of the rough ER and Golgi, so it builds nearly all of the neuron's proteins and ships them out along its extensions.
options: The axon has no nucleus; it receives its proteins from the cell body.
Dendrites are extensions of the cell body and rely on it for their proteins.
Axon terminals release chemicals, but the proteins they use were made in the cell body.
Correct. The cell body holds the nucleus and is the neuron's protein factory.

why.correct: A nerve is a cable of many axons. Some carry feeling in from the skin; others carry commands out to muscles and glands. Cutting the nerve cuts both kinds at once.
options: Correct. One nerve carries axons running both inward and outward.
The cell bodies of these neurons are not in the wrist; they lie in or near the spinal cord. The cut severed their axons.
Muscle injury does not remove feeling from the skin. Numbness points to cut axons.
Glial cells support neurons; the neurons themselves carry the signals.

why.correct: A nerve is an organ-level cable: the axons of many neurons, bundled together with connective tissue and blood vessels, running outside the brain and spinal cord.
options: A neuron is one cell. A nerve holds the axons of many neurons.
The cell bodies and dendrites lie elsewhere; a nerve carries axons.
Correct. A nerve is a bundle of axons wrapped in connective tissue.
Glial cells are found in nerves too, but a nerve is defined by its bundled axons, and it runs outside the brain.

why.correct: Glial cells support, insulate, feed and protect neurons. Neurons, not glia, carry the long-distance signals.
options: Correct. Some glial cells wrap axons, which speeds signals along them.
Neurons carry long-distance signals along their axons. Glia support that work.
Correct. Glia take up excess ions and chemicals from around neurons.
Correct. Some glial cells engulf debris and microbes.
Correct. Glia give nervous tissue its structure and hold neurons in place.

why.correct: A tumor grows from cells that divide out of control. Mature neurons do not divide, but glial cells keep that ability, so most cancerous tumors that start in brain tissue arise from glia.
options: Mature neurons do not divide, so they are an unlikely source of a tumor.
Fibroblasts belong to connective tissue. The question asks about a tumor that began in the brain tissue itself.
A nerve is a bundle of axons that runs outside the brain and spinal cord, not a dividing cell.
Correct. Glial cells can divide, so they are the usual source.

why.correct: The axon carries the signal away from the cell body, out to the axon terminals. Bringing signals toward the cell body is the dendrites' job.
options: This step is right: dendrites receive incoming signals.
This step is right: the cell body adds up the incoming signals.
This is the error. The axon carries the signal away from the cell body.
This step is right: axon terminals release chemicals by exocytosis.
This step is right: the chemicals act on the next cell.

why.correct: The cell body makes nearly all of a neuron's proteins, and they are carried along the axon to where they are needed. A piece of axon cut off from its cell body loses that supply and breaks down.
options: Correct. Cut off from the cell body, the far piece loses its protein supply.
Glial cells do not donate nuclei to axons. Without its own nucleus, the far piece cannot make new proteins.
Blood does not enter axons. The far piece breaks down because it has no protein supply.
The cell body is the supply, not the cause. The far piece breaks down because it is cut off from it.

why.correct: Neurons burn oxygen and glucose fast and store almost no fuel, so a few minutes without blood flow starts to kill them. Mature neurons do not divide, so those that die are mostly not replaced.
options: Glial cells help supply neurons with fuel; they do not block oxygen.
A neuron has one nucleus. The number of nuclei is not the issue.
Nervous tissue in the brain has a rich blood supply. The problem was that the blood stopped flowing.
Correct. High demand, no reserve and no division make neurons especially vulnerable.

why.correct: Dendrites receive signals, and each branch offers more places for other neurons' axon terminals to make contact. A huge dendrite tree can receive input from many thousands of neurons.
options: Distance depends on the axon's length, not on the dendrites.
Mature neurons do not divide, however branched they are.
Chemicals are released from axon terminals, not from dendrites.
Correct. More dendrite branches mean more incoming contacts.

why.correct: An axon terminal is a swollen knob at the tip of an axon branch, close to the next cell. An arriving signal makes it release chemicals by exocytosis, and those chemicals act on the next cell.
options: Correct. Axon terminals release chemicals onto the next cell.
Signals travel one way; they leave through the terminals and do not reverse.
Neither mature neurons nor their parts divide.
A signal is passed on at the terminal, not stored there.

why.correct: Glial wrapping insulates axons and speeds signals. Remove it and the signal slows, so it takes longer to reach the axon terminals, even before any axons are lost.

variables.name: Insulation around the axons
variables.why: The wrapping is layers of glial membrane that insulate the axon; destroying it removes the insulation.

variables.name: Speed of signals along the axons
variables.why: Insulating wrapping makes signals travel much faster, so losing it slows them.

variables.name: Number of axons in the region (at first)
variables.why: The question says the axons are left intact at first, so their number has not changed yet.

variables.name: Time for a signal to reach the axon terminals
variables.why: A slower signal takes longer to cover the same length of axon.

why.correct: Dendr- means tree. Dendrites branch again and again from the cell body, like the branches of a tree.
options: Correct. Dendr- = tree, matching their branching shape.
Axis is the meaning of axon, the single long extension.
Glue is the meaning of glia, the root that names the support cells.
Neur- means nerve. It is the root of neuron, not dendrite.

why.correct: Counts that dissolve brain tissue and count the nuclei find about 86 billion neurons and a similar number of other cells, mostly glia: a ratio near one to one overall, with big differences between regions. The older ten-to-one figure is still repeated in some textbooks.
options: This is the older, often repeated figure. Direct counts do not support it, though some exams still expect it.
Neurons do not outnumber glia this heavily in the brain as a whole.
Correct. Overall, the numbers are roughly equal.
Glial cells persist and keep dividing throughout life.

why.correct: A nerve is a bundle of axons, and the glial cells that wrap them, with connective tissue that carries blood vessels. The cell bodies of those neurons lie in or near the spinal cord, not in the nerve.
options: The cell bodies sit in or near the brain and spinal cord. A nerve carries only their axons.
A nerve holds thousands of axons from thousands of neurons, not one cell.
Correct. Axons, glial cells, connective tissue and blood vessels make up a nerve.
Signals move along axons by electrical changes, not by muscle. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart.
